posts.title: Ask HN: Anthropic is accusing my company of distilling. How can I prove I'm not?
posts.text: Basically the title. Anthropic is accusing me and my company of using their API for distillation. We are not. We do not train our own models. Our only usage which I think could get us flagged is automated regression benchmarks whenever we change some AI settings. But this is not against their policy? Now I've got 24h to prove we didn't. Has anyone dealt with this too? How can you prove that you are not distilling Anthropic models without breaking your user's privacy?

comments.text: Whatever you submit in 24h, submit the same evidence to Claude and ask it to tell you if it's sufficient evidence to make distilling seem unlikely. Because you know Anthropic is just going to be using Claude as well. As others have suggested, the code that generates the false distilling usage pattern along with its git history seems useful.

posts.title: Ask HN: Am I the only one whose AI hype is cooling down a lot?
posts.text: I am in the industry for 15+ years, studied CS, and actually, never really "liked" programming. It was a means to an end. I have written about programming (and published books), so don't get me wrong: I like the craft and I miss the sense of accomplishment after hours and days of struggling and fixing a problem with 2 lines of code. What I see in my personal spending and habits: I get free tokens from my company, and I spent between 3k-5k a month at the start of the year. Models got cheaper, but also: The usefullness ran its course a little bit for me. I still don't write code by hand, but when doing research, finding solutions, even some decisions (using Opus 5.5 and Astra 6.2 for example) are more and more questionable. I handed large research tasks to models, but even small questions like: "What do you think about these PR comments pointing out issues" (I need to be vague, working for a larger company), it didn't find even basic facts I found via Google and reading the docs for 2mins. I usually did higher level thinking, researched with the model, and then went to the implementation phase. But lately, I am not happy with both the research results (I continuesly have to narrow it down, go back, refine... I spend a day or 2 days refining, which in the end, I can do by myself now and actually feel a sense of accomplishment). Even the implementation isn't all that great. Maybe my bar for acceptable work is higher now, since these tools are not "magic" anymore. I think I gave them more leeway in the beginning because they wowed me. But now... not so much anymore. I even dread opening up Claude Code or Codex and I'd rather read and write code myself, and just give them smaller tasks, or once I nailed it down, I let a large chunk of code write by a model (because it "types" faster...). Am I alone? I read a lot of think pieces, I have agents working on my private dedicated server to maintain my machine and set up my self-hosting services. But more and more, I'd rather.... do it myself again, be more precise, and use it as a workhorse instead of a thinking researcher.

comments.text: It's important to separate out the models themselves from their implementation. For our internal research projects, AI has been completely hamstrung by our own poor data hygiene and technical debt. But for actually generating useful code I don't think I'll ever be able to go back. The fun of coding was the problem-solving - spending days banging your head against the wall because of a single typo is a frustration I feel no nostalgia for.

posts.title: Ask HN: Are the trades a safe career transition?
posts.text: I am a software guy. Engineering degree but not PEng. Im thinking of jumping ship because i dont see much of a future in the career. Ai has me a little discouraged I need a few decades of at least mild security to get to retirement... Are the trades safe? Im worried about homeowners and companies ending up with robots that do all those tasks. Not next year obviously, but it could happen before the career change fully pays off And if not the trades, then what is a better bet?

comments.text: If you look at a graph of the US economy, and remove software and data centers, there’s basically no growth. Don’t leave software. AI will change your job, but it won’t replace you, not even in multiple decades. Be strategic about the kinds of software roles you get into. Look for niches with stability. Look to go toward highly regulated software niches. For example, I work in an area where it would be impossible to remove manual testers due to certain regulations. Software work for government where you must be a US citizen or you must do specific things manually could be another example. I also think some areas are going to be more insulated from AI disruption. I think ops and security have more stability. Anything that requires more judgment and less “take inputs and turn them into outputs.” Moving from an upper middle class career track to something you can get into without a high school diploma is a mistake. In many trades you’re competing with dudes who are working under the table and aren’t even documented. Even if you’re not, they’re mostly hard on your body, and some aren’t even immune from automation.
comments.author: Grombobulous

comments.text: I’ve never worked as a professional tradesman, but I’ve done quite a bit of that type of work. It’s hard. It’s hard on your body in ways that will become more of an issue as you age. It’s also, imho, very satisfying work. But it’s tough. And even though you might look at your last plumbing bill and say “damn, that would be good money!” the reality is that very few in the trades will bring all of that home themselves. As for AI in the software field… I’ve watched the people around me. Some of them are doing good work with AI. And what they all have in common is serious skill and experience predating AI. What it looks like from my seat is that AI in software dev and related fields is absolutely a force multiplier… but only for people who already know what they’re doing. So as a few other people have said, don’t be too hasty to jump ship. There may yet be some good opportunities. Btw, having said all of that, my AI use is limited to summarizing searches and assisting on code review. I’m personally quite “anti AI” and close enough to retirement that if eventually I can’t keep up without going all-in, I’m ok with being fired. Love my job and the people I work with, though.
comments.author: allenrb

comments.text: AI is definitely changing things a lot in the field, but don't discount the massive change in how cheap money was during ZIRP and how expensive it became after ZIRP finally ended. This was coincidentally around the same time the layoffs in big tech started, which was before AI really had any meaningful impact. When money is cheap it is a lot easier for companies to hire, and when money suddenly stops being cheap it is a lot harder. In particular, large discontinuities in economic conditions, which we just experienced recently post-covid, always produce downturns in affected industries (which is distinct from the first order aspect of how expensive money is). So I think even ignoring AI we could expect several years of down-ness and reorganization followed by a recovery. I don't think we can even tell this point if AI will reduce demand for developers. The economy for software might be even worse right now if the AI developments hadn't happened when they did, there was an insane hiring spree during COVID and even before that the industry employment-side was growing at a probably unsustainable pace.
comments.author: pfannkuchen

comments.text: Something to keep in mind in these kind of discussions: the most pessimistic visions of the future are not worth preparing for on an individual level even if they end up materializing. This is because apocalyptic problems can only be reasonably addressed with solutions that are very large-scale and political in nature, and trying to minimise your own personal exposure is akin to doomsday prepping. If the doomers are right and AI fully automates knowledge work leaving most unable to produce much value, the entire notion of a 'safe career path' doesn’t make sense. Not just because of robotics, but also because demand for even the safest bets likely collapses in such a scenario. And honestly, in this case there would be far more pressing issues than long term job security. IMO, make decisions like these based on what fulfils you rather than out of fear.

comments.text: Trades are boom bust even more so than software engineering. There is a shortage, people run to the field, but by the time they are trained up (end of apprenticeship) there is probably a bust because there are too many people in them. You need to be prepared to sweat out at least one bust at the beginning of your career, and stay in it so you can reap a boom or two. comments.text: Start with the realization that unless you are just plain lucky (as a result of birth for example), security is something that is usually self made. Regardless of the industry, wage slavery is insecure by design . The threat of losing your job is ever present and used as a motivating factor. Even when it is not being overtly stated, it remains an option that is never far away from being utilized. Real security is control over your own destiny. And the only way I know to achieve a reasonable measure of it by running your own business. It doesn't really matter what kind of business but I'd recommend something you have some natural interest in. Just as an example, I know a guy with lots of financial security. He owns a string of barber shops and hair salons. He started out by learning to cut hair but nowadays, the only thing he cuts is checks to his employees --- while taking a sizeable "cut" for himself. If AI robots learn how to cut hair, he has the money to invest in some, adapt and continue on with his business. This is called "security".

comments.text: The answer is nuanced: https://prentice.training/data-centers/ Everyone likes an abstract answer. But the reality is often career switchers need money and a career path now. No one really cares about what will happen in 10 years. Careers like electricians and plumbing will - most likely for the the next decade - require human input. You need to take an adversarial - what would you need to believe - style approach: * Do you have a household robot with sufficient dexterity and intelligence to work with electric circuits? Does EVERYONE? * Does that robot have a way of getting wire and parts to a sight reliably, everywhere you could imagine? * Does that robot have agency to perform permitted work (a POLITICAL question, btw)? * etc. You'll see that tradespeople, for roughly a decade at least, will be in good standing. Self-driving cars, despite the technology being largely safer and performant, are still in infancy. Imagine robots in your home. Imagine a safety accident. The main issue is whether anyone is getting rich doing anything post robot and AI takeover, but it will at least be something to do.

comments.text: Trades are very cyclical and offer little in the way of a safety net. You'll have fat and lean years. The ones who are the most successful are the ones who can stick and move and are unsentimental about what work they are doing.

comments.text: The way to think about this is what are you actually producing. If you are able to find work where you actually build real software products you are probably ok. I am frequently seeing new companies pitch work to me about their team using AI to build some product. Again, if AI is doing the work then what do I need that company for when I could just use AI to build the same thing myself? AI is not the problem. It’s just accelerating a problem that was already present: most people hired to write software cannot write software. I have seen people aggressively defend this incompetence for the last two decades. Even as the jobs are shrinking people are still aggressively defending their inability to write software because it qualifies their existence just pumping out React templates in an industry that values hiring/firing over any product.

posts.text: I'm Senior software engineer in the US (DMV area), with 15y of experience. Worked for Fortune 50+ company and bunch of mid-size companies. Been unemployed for 2y and can't find a job, within those 2 years, I pretty much spent my savings that I've saved through years, maybe have 4-5 months left to support my household. Currently, I tutor math and probably about to start working as manager in pizzaria. In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. At this point, I have massive gap in my resume that I can't explain to recruiters, I can still code (C#/.NET/AWS) and learned the AI, but who cares if date of my last employment is Jan2025. What should I do ? If you have an alternative path (something completely different from SWE or SWE adjacent) that pays "well", I would like to hear.

comments.text: > In Jan 2025, I quit from a mid-size insurance tech company(1000+) after working there for almost 4y, because I was tipped off the they were about to start layoffs and they did. Well, since then I have zero luck finding any job in SWE. I don't know the OP's circumstances. What I am about to say is meant as advice to others and not a criticism of the OP. If you suspect that you may be the target of a layoff, DO NOT SIMPLY QUIT. In this scenario you are a potential liability to your employer. They will almost certainly pay you to leave if they decide to part ways. It is always easier to find a job when you have a job. Maybe you think if there are layoffs and you are retained that it will be a miserable working environment. Fine. DO NOT QUIT. After a round of layoffs you are relatively safe and you can use that time to find another job. It is very likely that layoffs are going to continue as companies restructure because of AI. Have a plan. Keep your wits and hold fast.
comments.author: powvans

comments.text: I had to get back into the industry last year after 4 years off for mental health and caregiving. I was able to get back in - 2 years isn’t that much. But the problem is the front door in hiring is broken. Entirely. I didn’t receive almost ANY replies from hundreds of sent out resumes - I have household names and big public high scale launches and wins on my resume, but no FAANG and no degree. I got 2 job offers. One was through a manager from 8 years prior who was working at a place. One was a recruiter who found me on LinkedIn. I got engagement when someone physically actually knew me, they were actually hiring, and my skills overlapped. My honest advice is to apply places and try that dance, get yourself in front of people, real people, and mainly 1-1. Work everyone you have ever worked with. If you’ve reviewed their PR, they need to know that you need a job. Be kind and genuinely catch up with them if you want to, but they are your PRIMARY resource to get a job and you can’t let shame get in your way. Corporations in general are BROKEN right now in massive ways and the industry is going through a crisis. It will likely become better but whatever you have to do to survive do it. Finally, it seems like solutions architects seem in demand lately, anyone who can help customers with solutions - SWEs can tend to do well if you have some people skills.

comments.text: This is still the best article I've found on this subject: https://ludic.mataroa.blog/blog/ludics-guide-to-getting-soft... from one of my favourite bloggers, his other stuff is very worth reading. My take on it: the standard recruitment process is completely broken. Don't even start doing that. Sending applications to a job advert is an exercise in futility and will destroy your mental health. comments.text: I'd go the route of not answering calls from numbers I don't know, triaging my emails well and, in general, staying suspicious. So be aware, and don't trust anything you haven't confirmed yourself. Cause even if a Vendor says they removed everything from you, I would trust that all traces are removed. comments.text: The comments so far appear to be tackling external recruiters however I think you're actually asking about internal recruiters so I'll focus on that. Context: My career started in software engineering before moving into recruitment. I spent a few years agency-side (external) but the majority of my career has been internal (including with a few YC companies). I have about ~15yrs of experience ranging from tech recruiter to Global VP of Talent. Assessing recruiter skills (just like assessing an engineer's skills) varies from company to company. One of the most common metrics is 'time to hire' which is essentially a measure of how long it takes to go from a vacancy going live, to having someone in the seat. Ultimately that is the most useful measure because an ineffective recruiter will take much longer to fill an open role. For me, the next most important measure was essentially a hiring manager NPS. I appreciate you might assume that the candidate NPS is more important however I've found that people you've just given a job to tend to only provide positive feedback on the experience so it's a bit redundant. Another critical measure of efficacy for me is the interview success rate ratio. We'd look at every stage of our hiring pipeline and measure the pass/fail ratio with the goal being as close to a 50/50 split as possible. Having a balance is important because if everyone you interview is good enough to get through to the next stage then either your process is lacking rigour or your standards aren't high enough! This measure also tends to counter the whole "throw shit at the wall and see what sticks" approach. When you're an internal recruiter, one of the biggest values you add to a business is reducing the time the business spends on recruitment so less time interviewing poor quality candidates is critical. On the point of retention rates; I generally don't hold my recruiters accountable for that. Naturally we pay attention to any obvious negative trends but broadly speaking, it's the recruiters job to identify and attract good people, it's the hiring team and hiring managers responsibility to assess them and on-board them properly. It's my job to help the hiring team and hiring managers get better at retention. Happy to answer any other questions you have!

posts.title: Ask HN: Should Uber Ratings Decay over Time?
posts.text: I’ve been thinking about how platforms like Uber calculate reputation scores, and I believe there’s a fundamental flaw in how historical ratings are treated. Uber calculates passenger ratings using the last 500 rated trips, regardless of when those trips occurred. In my case, I have 455 ratings, 426 of which are five stars (93.6%). My overall rating is 4.86. What bothers me isn’t the score itself, but the underlying methodology. A negative rating from five years ago can carry exactly the same weight as one received yesterday. And if you’re an infrequent user who hasn’t accumulated 500 ratings, that negative feedback could influence your reputation for years. This raises an interesting question: Should reputation systems measure your historical average, or should they attempt to represent who you are today? One possible solution is exponential time decay: Weight = 2^(-t/H) Where t is the age of the rating and H is a half-life, perhaps 12 months. Under that approach, a rating from one year ago would carry 50% of its original weight, and one from two years ago just 25%. Of course, this introduces other challenges. How do you prevent someone with a history of poor behaviour from simply waiting for their reputation to recover? How do you maintain statistical confidence for infrequent users? Would Bayesian smoothing or a minimum effective sample size help? There’s also a broader philosophical question around the right to be forgotten. Should digital reputation systems indefinitely preserve the consequences of historical assessments, particularly when those assessments are subjective and potentially no longer representative? I’m curious how others would approach this. * Is a rolling window of 500 ratings statistically defensible without considering time? * Would exponential decay produce a fairer and more predictive reputation score? * Should platforms expose both a lifetime rating and a recent-behaviour rating? * Are there better approaches already being used in other reputation systems? I’d be particularly interested in perspectives from people who’ve worked on marketplace ranking, trust and safety, or reputation algorithms. It seems like a relatively simple mathematical change, but one with potentially significant implications for fairness across digital platforms.

posts.title: Ask HN: Are startups today worth it even in a best case scenario?
posts.text: I'm gonna open this with the disclaimer that this is purely a financial and risk comparison post. No one is complaining that we are poorly compensated. It is good to discuss compensation so we can make informed and educated decisions when deciding how to commit the next few years of our lives. A close friend of mine joined an AI startup (being intentionally vague) around 1.5 years ago and despite the company doing extremely well on valuation, I'm surprised at how he's not really better off than just working at a large tech company. Concrete numbers for the startup: -200k salary -Equity grant over 4 years is 500k -The company's valuation has since went from single billions to tens of billions, leaving him with a 10x multiplier when looking only at valuation. After you account for dilution, it's closer to 6x. -Liquidity event annually allows you to sell 10% of your vested shares Big tech at a similar years of experience is around 400-500k total comp, and the RSU component is generally liquid. For example sake and ease of calculation, if you assume that my friend's entire equity was vested, and he was able to sell 10% of it, it would amount to approximately $300k/liquidity event, which brings him to around 500k a year as well (200k + 300k). In reality, he's really only able to access $300k/4 since that's all he has vested and that brings him closer to $75k for this liquidity event. There are a lot of variables I'm leaving out obviously such as potential future value, IPO, etc., but the thing that is surprising to me overall is that this is a close to best case outcome, yet the employee doesn't really end up any better off than big tech due to lack of liquidity and dilution. I mean I get it, impact, interesting work, etc. -- the qualitative measures -- aren't really accounted for, but I'm not looking to make a wholistic comparison. This brings me to the question: Is the risk in a startup ever justified for a lower level employee (engineer, Product Manager, Program Manager, etc.)?

It is one thing for an LLM to understand when it needs to run a bash script to collect some system info. It is another thing entirely to expect it to be able to take an image, process it, understand depth/distance, map that delta to some co-ordinate system, then call the exact correct motor functions with the right parameters to cover that distance, ( not accounting for positioning hand to correctly grip and pickup the object of arbitrary shape) grab the item and return home. TLDR, agentic AI for programming today is still leaps and bounds behind a consistent realistic AI body.
